title: NP-completeness of aggregate root-dependent spanning-tree cost
strongest_verified: The explicitly encoded common undirected spanning-tree decision problem charging every arc in every rooted whole-tree orientation is NP-complete even with nonnegative costs in{0,1,2}.
The same decision problem is strongly NP-complete because the reduction uses bounded costs and threshold K<=2N, and its positive-shift{1,2,3} corollary is strongly NP-complete.

The entire proof includes polynomial normalization/output construction, universal structural forcing, exact structured literal-root identity, both satisfiability directions, NP verification and bit-length/unary controls.
central_gap_or_counterexample: None found for the literal theorem and corollary under their written finite explicit input model. Finite controls corroborate but do not supply NP-hardness.
necessary_hypotheses: One common undirected spanning tree on a finite simple connected graph; N>=1.
All root cost vectors are freely independently supplied and charge every oriented tree edge; the explicit table has2N|E| entries.
The NP-completeness statement uses finitely encoded nonnegative integer costs and integer threshold.
The reduction source is at-most-three-literal CNF with polynomial truth-preserving normalization and dense occurring variable labels.
The structural proof uses nonnegative remaining root costs and the written B=2 table; its auxiliary B>=2 identity is supported.
exclusions_and_boundaries: Separately optimized root trees, terminal-path-only objectives and KaibelProblem2 are different and not settled.
The theorem is not a claim that arbitrary unencoded real-number inputs lie in NP.
Symmetric root tables yield an ordinary edge-additive MST objective; clause-root asymmetry is substantive.
Structured literal-count formula is not asserted for arbitrary trees or unrestricted global optimum.
At B=1 the stated q-penalty disappears; no conclusion for that modified construction is claimed.
Inward orientation requires table transposition; a false-literal exact control detects omitting it.
